title: Acceptance and rising
hookLine: bhaana and chardi kala held together
tomorrow: Bebe asks Arjan's family's last name. why would that matter?

cards: Half a win can feel worse than a loss. The junior from the bus stop gets a detention and has to apologize to Arjan in person. Good.
But the thing Simran actually asked for, a lunch-hour turban day where anyone at school could learn to tie one, gets a polite no. Not this year, too close to finals, maybe next spring.
She reads it in the parking lot and texts the family chat a single word: cool. Everyone who knows her knows that cool means the opposite. Bebe replies with one word too: bhaana.
Simran stares at it. Is that wisdom, or is it giving up?

teach.h: BHAANA: WHAT HAPPENED, IN THE WILL.
teach.b: Bhaana means the Will: what has happened, inside the order of the One.

teach.h: NO ONE STANDS OUTSIDE THE HUKAM.
teach.b: The Japji says, in its second pauri on Ang 1, in paraphrase: everyone is within the hukam, the order; no one stands outside it. So the no from the school is real. It happened.
Pretending it didn't, or burning energy raging at it, doesn't change it. Guru Arjan goes further on Ang 394. In paraphrase: what you do seems sweet to me.
But accepting what happened is not the same as approving of it, and it is never the same as quitting.

teach.h: CHARDI KALA: THE GOOD OF ALL.
teach.b: The other half is chardi kala, rising spirits, the spirit that keeps climbing.
And the two are held in one breath at the end of the Ardas, the prayer that closes Sikh gatherings: with the Name, rising spirits; in your Will, the good of all. Sarbat da bhala.
Here's the part to tell a friend tonight: that closing line doesn't ask for good things for Sikhs only. It asks for the good of all. So: accept the no.
Then rise. Simran doesn't get her school-wide day. She does have a lunch table, Arjan, Maya, and a bag of practice cloth in her dad's truck.

how: Sikhs close the Ardas, said at the end of gatherings and in daily prayer, by asking for rising spirits with the Name and the good of all within the Will.

o: taking what happened as the Will, then rising to what's next
giving up on a goal because God has already decided it
staying cheerful by not thinking about what went wrong

p: the order no one stands outside

s: accepting the Will means you stop trying
bhaana is held together with chardi kala: accept what happened, then rise to what's yours.
the Ardas ends by asking for the good of all, not only of Sikhs
with the Name, rising spirits; in your Will, sarbat da bhala, the good of all.
the Japji says no one stands outside the hukam
the second pauri, on Ang 1, in paraphrase: everyone is within the order.

games.q: you tried out for varsity and got put on JV instead. going by today, what does 'accept, then rise' look like?
o: take the JV spot fully, and ask the coach what to work on next.
quit the team, since it clearly wasn't meant to be this season.
say yes to JV, but keep arguing the decision until it changes.
games.why: bhaana: the decision happened, so accept it. chardi kala: rise to the next step that's yours. accepting isn't approving, and it's never quitting.

practice: Bring to mind one thing that didn't go your way this week. Say quietly what part of it you can't change, and let that part be. Then name one small next step that's still yours, and when you'll take it.

wordCard.voice: Acceptance and rising. Bhaana and chardi kala, held together: accept what happened, then rise to the next thing that's yours to do.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: bhaana, the Will, what happens within the order of the One.

carryVoice: Keep this one: accept, then rise, in that order, like the end of the Ardas. One lunch table, a bag of cloth, and day 1727.

sources.ref: Ang 1, Japji, second pauri ('hukmai andar sabh ko, baahar hukam na koe'), paraphrased
Ang 394, Raag Asa, Guru Arjan ('tera kia meetha laagai'), paraphrased
Ardas, closing lines ('Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhaane sarbat da bhala'), paraphrased
